title: A dated benchmark of NPOV disputes on English Wikipedia, and what it says about catching bias early
content:
Wikipedia’s neutral point of view (NPOV) is one of its founding principles, and editors enforce it in part with maintenance templates, the {{POV}} banner and its relatives that flag an article (or a section) as disputed. A natural question follows: could a tool watch articles and catch one sliding away from neutrality before an editor has to flag it? That was the premise we set out to test. The answer turned out to be more interesting than a yes or no.

Most of the work was getting the ground truth right. Dating an NPOV dispute is harder than it looks:

  • Bots backdate templates. About 26% of dated maintenance templates were last touched by a bot stamping them with a month. If you date the dispute by the template alone, you’re measuring the bot’s run, not when a human actually raised the concern.
  • Edit summaries miss half the story. Searching edit summaries for tag additions recovers only about 53% of the human edits that really added a template.
  • Controls can be dormant. If you compare a tagged article to a “similar” article matched only on lifetime totals, the comparison article is often inactive in the exact window your detector looks at, which quietly flatters the results.

title: Call for Applications: Wiki for Minorities Mentorship Program Cohort 1
content:
Are you passionate about minority communities, languages, cultures, cultural heritage, religious minorities, disability communities, and other underrepresented voices across Wikimedia projects?

Wiki for Minorities (WfMin) is pleased to announce the opening of applications for Cohort 1 of the WfMin Mentorship Program. The program is designed to support Wikimedia contributors and community members who are working to strengthen the visibility and representation of minority and minoritized languages, people with disabilities, religious minorities, cultural communities, and other underrepresented groups across Wikimedia projects,

You can apply as either a Mentor or Mentee:

🔹 Mentors: Share your knowledge, experience, and skills with emerging contributors.

🔹 Mentees: Learn from experienced Wikimedians, develop new skills, and receive guidance for your Wikimedia journey.

Application Period: 25th October 2026 – 5th November 2026.

📝 Apply here (Google Form)

We look forward to welcoming passionate contributors from across the Wikimedia movement and building a stronger network for minority communities together.

title: Why Wikimedia Is Speaking Up in a Major AI Copyright Case
content:
The Wikimedia Foundation has filed an amicus brief, a “friend of the court” submission, with the Southern District Court of New York in In re: OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation, a major copyright case involving OpenAI and Microsoft. The Foundation’s goal is to help protect the open, accessible knowledge that Wikipedia, and millions of people, depend on.

The case brings together 12 lawsuits, the most well-known of them being The New York Times Co. v Microsoft and OpenAI. At its heart is an important question: When AI companies use copyrighted information does it qualify as fair use?

For the Wikimedia Foundation, the answer needs to leave room for innovation while supporting the people and organizations that make access to knowledge possible, including Wikimedia volunteers. The Foundation is not taking the side of either OpenAI or The New York Times in this case. It is asking the court to protect open knowledge, something that matters to everyone who uses the internet.

title: From Wikipedia to the Wikimedia movement: making free knowledge easier to share
content:
What if sharing an interesting Wikimedia fact did not require a design tool, a QR-code generator and a separate caption? Wiki DYK Share Tool (wiki-dyk.toolforge.org) turns content from supported Wikimedia pages into ready-to-share images with QR codes, captions and customizable hashtags. It can also help communities promote campaigns, events and initiatives without requiring graphic-design skills.

In October 2025, the Wikimedia Foundation reported that human pageviews on Wikipedia had declined by approximately 8% compared with the same months in 2024. The Foundation pointed to changing online habits, including AI-generated answers in search engines and younger audiences increasingly turning to social video platforms for information. Read the Wikimedia Foundation’s update.

For those of us who contribute to Wikimedia projects, this raises an important question: how can we help more people discover the knowledge our communities create?

Every day, volunteers write articles, upload photographs, improve dictionaries, digitize historical documents, contribute structured data and organize community events. Yet much of this work remains unfamiliar to people outside our communities.

title: Bringing Wikimedia to a Remote Island
content: Matsu (Traditional Chinese:馬祖) is a group of islands administered by Taiwan but located very close to mainland China. The islands are commonly referred to as the “four townships and five islands,” reflecting the local administrative divisions and major islands. Separated from Taiwan by the Taiwan Strait, Matsu can only be reached by air or sea, making it quite a challenge to bring Wikimedia movement there. Fortunately, a senior Taiwanese Wikimedia organizer, who previously served on the board of Wikimedia Taiwan, now lives and works in Matsu. Through his efforts, a local community development project has incorporated Wikimedia into its activities.

title: “Don’t Blink”: Protecting the Wikimedia model, its people, and its values in September 2026
content:
Welcome to “Don’t Blink”! Every month we share public policy developments from around the world that shape people’s ability to participate in the free knowledge movement. In case you blinked last month, here are the most important advocacy topics that have kept the Wikimedia Foundation busy.

The Global Advocacy team works to advocate laws and government policies that protect the volunteer community-led Wikimedia model, Wikimedia’s people, and the Wikimedia movement’s core values.

To learn more about us and the work we do with the rest of the Foundation: follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky; sign up for our quarterly newsletter or Wikimedia public policy mailing list; and visit our Meta-Wiki webpage.

title: Africa Restitution Knowledge: Quality, Research and Discovery
content:
Have you ever created an article, but there were not enough sources to improve it, left it for a while, then months later found exactly the kind of resources you had been looking for? Yes, that was me with Ngonnso.

The Africa Restitution Knowledge Project focused on improving public knowledge about African restitution efforts through high-quality contributions to Wikipedia and Wikidata. It began when Olubusola Afolabi, the Community Engagement Lead at Free Knowledge Africa (FKA), reached out and mentioned that the project was in partnership with Open Restitution Africa (ORA). I knew that name sounded familiar. I went back to look at my contributions history and voila! I found out that while creating articles about individuals working on reparations, I had also created articles connected to ORA, restitution, the Ngonnso statue, and some of the African cultural objects that need to be returned. It was an easy YES.

title: Sulaymaniyah Through a Wiki Lens 2026
content:
Seven students. Five places. One city with stories waiting to be told. On 17 October 2026, we grabbed our cameras and phones and set out to show Sulaymaniyah to the world, one free photo at a time. Here is how Sulaymaniyah Through a Wiki Lens 2026 went from an idea to a day we will not forget.

Sulaymaniyah is often called the cultural capital of Kurdistan. It is a city of poets and artists, of busy bazaars and squares that have seen history unfold. So here is a question: if you searched for it on Wikimedia Commons, what would you find?

The honest answer was: not enough. Many of the city’s best-known places had only a handful of photos, and some Wikipedia articles about them had no image at all. A reader on the other side of the world could read about Sulaymaniyah’s old bazaars without ever seeing one. That felt like something we could fix.

Every good project needs the right team, and we had one waiting at the American University of Iraq, Sulaimani. The AUIS Wikimedia Student Club is the first university club established by Wikimedia Iraq, and its members are curious, creative and ready to get involved.
snippet: Seven students. Five places. One city with stories waiting to be told. On 17 October 2026, we grabbed our cameras and phones and set out to show Sulaymaniyah to the world, one free photo at a time.

title: My all-inclusive experience at the inaugural Language Diversity Conference 2026 held in Accra, Ghana
content:
The inaugural edition of the Language Diversity Conference in Accra, Ghana, was more than an opportunity to discuss language preservation and open knowledge. For me, it was also an opportunity to serve, meet people from different language communities, explore Ghana’s rich history, and experience the country’s cultural diversity through food, photography, and sightseeing.

Held under the theme “Strengthening Language Communities in the Open Knowledge Movement,” the three-day conference from 2nd – 4th October, 2026, brought together participants from different backgrounds, united by a common interest in making knowledge more inclusive and accessible. While the presentations and discussions were central to the event, some of my most memorable experiences happened outside the conference sessions.

One of my roles during the conference was volunteering at the registration desk. Although registration may seem like a small part of organizing an event, it is often the first point of contact for participants and plays an important role in shaping their experience.

title: Traveling to celebrate Wikipedia’s 25th birthday? Baby Globe is doing it, with geocaching
content:
Group photo of the Wikipedia25 meetup in Bologna, Italy
Photo by Danysan1 published under the license CC-BY-SA 4.0

This summer was marked by record-breaking heat, a far cry from the cool weather that greeted us in May at ExDynamo in Bologna, Italy, where we celebrated Wikipedia’s 25th birthday together with not one but two plushes of Baby Globes, the charming mascot of the year.

This hot summer, I came up with a wild idea, perhaps the result of heatstroke (who knows?): why not mash up my current favorite hobbies, to have some fun and keep the Wikipedia25 celebrations going on?

For those who don’t know me, I’ve been active on the Wikimedia projects for many years, and for a few years now on OpenStreetMap too. In 2026, I also (re)discovered geocaching by joining the ‘Tortellini in bro’ team, a sort of informal group of Sunday wanderers and GPS-equipped treasure hunters. (As you may have guessed, yes, ‘bro’ is about ‘brotherhood’, but also ‘tortellini in broth‘, a local and traditional recipe.)

In a broad sense, these hobbies (Wikimedia projects, OpenStreetMap and geocaching) are all connected, or at least they are for me.

title: Building a Technical Community in Latin America: Get to Know the LATAM Technical Community Calls
content:
The Wikimedia movement has a vibrant community of people who develop tools, reuse data, maintain infrastructure, and contribute to the technological development of our projects. However, in Latin America, it has not always been easy to find spaces where we can connect, share experiences, and discuss the technical and sociotechnical challenges facing our region.

Following conversations among Wikimedians from different countries, the LATAM Technical Community Calls began in April 2026. This collaborative initiative aims to connect people interested in Wikimedia technologies, share knowledge, and strengthen regional collaboration.

Before these calls began, many of our opportunities to meet happened during international events, such as the Wikimedia Hackathon. Paradoxically, people from neighboring Latin American countries often found themselves meeting thousands of kilometers away from our region. While these gatherings have been essential for building community connections, we recognized the need for a more permanent and accessible space to stay in touch and work together on shared interests.

title: Around the Globe: Meet the joy-nitiatives across the Wikimedia movement
content:
Things you expect when joining Wikipedia and the Wikimedia movement? Laptops, sources and citations, debates, policies and infoboxes. 

Things you don’t expect? Karaoke, weddings, catchy songs, celebrations, friends, and candy (So. Much. Candy). 

Yes, Wikipedia exists to share free, neutral and reliable knowledge. But this mission is fueled by people: curious, generous, and passionate. And with that kind of people, joy sparks pretty much naturally.

A careful observer of the Wikimedia movement soon notices that joy is an underlying thread, running through almost everything that we do, on our projects and at our events, in every corner of the wikiworld. 

In this blogpost we tried to gather some of it but be warned:

title: Beyond articles: How Language Diversity Hub’s mentorship is helping 13 language communities grow in Wikimedia
content:
From technical skills and new leadership structures to institutional partnerships and Wikipedia milestones, the Language Diversity Hub Mentorship Programme is showing what sustained, community-centred support can make possible.

Creating articles is part of the answer. But communities also need technical skills, supportive leadership, institutional partnerships, funding opportunities, and the confidence to keep going when challenges arise.

These needs are at the heart of the Language Diversity Hub (LDH) Mentorship Programme, which supports language communities at different stages of developing and sustaining their Wikimedia projects.

The programme’s August 2026 report captures the progress of 13 language communities across Africa, Asia, and the Americas. After the first six months of the 12-month programme cycle, the results demonstrated the value of combining personalised mentorship with practical training, micro-grants, and opportunities for communities to learn from one another.

The programme has recorded encouraging progress across content creation, editor participation, technical capacity, and community governance.
